title: Remarks at Dickinson, North Dakota
paragraphs: I am more pleased than I can say to come back and have a chance to see you. The farther west I have gotten to-day, the more I have felt as if I was coming home. (Applause) It is just seventeen years ago that I came over here as orator of the day at the Fourth of July celebration. I remember it just as well as can be.

Now I want to say one word, especially, Captain to you and the members of the guard who have come down to greet me. Naturally, I have a peculiar feeling toward you. We have been comrades in effect together, (Applause)

There are a great many of you here whom I knew in the old days when I used to bring my cattle in to ship them from here. And in those days I do not think there was a puncher in the country that had not worked for me.

I do not know if you recollect once when I was a deputy sheriff and I brought in three men (A voice "I do")-- somebody says that he was one of them, but I am sure that is not so--and naturally I come back here and I feel that I am among my old friends, the people whom I knew so well. All I regret is that I cannot spend a couple of hours shaking hands and talking over the past with you.

Knowing North Dakota so well, I have watched all that she has done in the growth of the state with peculiar interest. I am proud of your success. I am proud of the way you have earned it. The changes since I first came to Dickinson, which was twenty years ago, have been great. When I first came to Bismarck, the railroad did not come this far. Twenty years ago I first struck Medora; and one of your citizens repaired my rifle, with which I killed my first buffalo. I wish I could stay here permanently
